Microbiota-Bile acid decoupling contributes to altered postnatal growth and metabolism in sFGR: a twin-paired dynamic study with FMT validation.

This study uses monochorionic diamniotic twin pairs to show that selective fetal growth restriction (sFGR) is associated with a decoupling between gut microbiota and bile acid metabolism, which may drive adverse postnatal growth and metabolic outcomes. By integrating metagenomics, 16S rRNA sequencing, metabolomics, and fecal microbiota transplantation validation, the authors identify early-life microbiota-bile acid perturbations as a potential mechanism underlying sFGR-associated long-term health risks.

Fecal microbiota transplantation in cancer immunotherapy: targeting the Gut-Tumor Axis.

This review evaluates clinical evidence for fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) as an adjunct to immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) cancer therapy, focusing on its potential to improve efficacy and reduce treatment-related intestinal toxicity. It critically integrates fragmented clinical, ecological, and mechanistic data on the gut-tumor axis and discusses inconsistent responses and the limited predictive value of microbiome remodeling. The review highlights the need for standardized approaches and deeper mechanistic understanding to optimize FMT in immunotherapy.

Lung microbiota in COPD: a double-edged sword.

This review proposes a 'double-edged sword' framework for understanding the lung microbiota in COPD, arguing that its effects depend on community structure and ecological balance rather than on individual beneficial or pathogenic taxa. It synthesizes how immigration, elimination, local growth conditions, and host-environment interactions shape this low-biomass ecosystem and how COPD disrupts that equilibrium.

The authors profile regional spatial variation in host and microbial responses to zinc, aiming to explain why zinc supplementation trials have produced inconsistent outcomes. The work highlights that zinc's effects on the host-microbiome interface are region-specific rather than uniform along the gut.

The ecological impact of Ulva prolifera green tide outbreaks: microbial connectivity and metabolic divergence.

This study used amplicon and metagenomic sequencing to examine how Ulva prolifera green tides affect microbial community dynamics across microhabitats. The work reveals that green tides enhance microbial connectivity and drive metabolic divergence among microhabitats.

Complete coding sequence of a virus belonging to the Chaphamavirus genus identified in a pooled blood sample from Actitis macularius birds collected on the Brazilian Amazon coast.

The authors sequenced the complete coding region of a novel chaphamavirus from a pooled blood sample of spotted sandpipers (Actitis macularius) collected on the Brazilian Amazon coast. The genome is substantially divergent from known chaphamaviruses, indicating a distinct genetic lineage and suggesting that the genus may need taxonomic revision. This is a descriptive viral discovery report with limited functional or epidemiological follow-up.

iScience 2026-11-20 Medium

Multi-scale hybrid correction of noisy long reads.

DADEC is a new hybrid error-correction pipeline for noisy long reads that combines stringent de Bruijn graph correction, haplotype-aware short-read alignment refinement, and permissive de Bruijn graph recovery in a confidence-ordered framework. Across seven simulated and three real datasets, it achieved the lowest mismatch and indel rates in most benchmarks while avoiding over-correction of genuine biological variation. The method targets the trade-off between suppressing sequencing errors and preserving true haplotype diversity.

Genome-resolved multi-omics characterizes bacterial, viral, and metabolic components associated with Parkinson's disease gut ecosystem variation.

This study combined deep shotgun metagenomic sequencing with fecal metabolomics in a high-altitude cohort of Parkinson's disease patients and matched spouse controls, reconstructing 455 species-level bacterial genome bins and 2,957 viral operational taxonomic units. The genome-resolved multi-omics approach links bacterial, viral, and metabolic features to variation in the PD gut ecosystem, providing a higher-resolution view of gut-brain axis components than prior 16S-based studies.

Urban avian viromes reveal viral diversity of potential public health relevance across China.

This study performed a large-scale viromic survey of birds across 22 Chinese cities, identifying over 52,000 viral operational taxonomic units and revealing extensive, previously underexplored viral diversity in urban avian communities. Viral richness varied markedly among cities, driven largely by bacteriophage diversity, while vertebrate-associated viruses showed a narrower range. The findings highlight how urbanization shapes viral diversity at the human-animal interface and identify viruses of potential public health relevance.

Aerobic and anaerobic cultivation shapes steroid-degrading wastewater consortia: Metagenomic insights into catabolic potential and antibiotic resistance genes.

This study enriched microbial consortia from dairy and municipal wastewater on progesterone (P4) and 17β-estradiol (E2) under aerobic and anaerobic conditions, coupling degradation kinetics with shotgun metagenomics. Aerobic consortia removed >99% of P4 within 9–12 h and E2 within 24 h, far outperforming anaerobic cultures, and metagenomic analysis linked these differences to catabolic gene potential and antibiotic resistance gene profiles. The work shows that cultivation condition and wastewater source strongly shape steroid-degrading community function and associated resistance risks.

The approach aims to improve accuracy in diet-health association studies where parental recall is unreliable.

The OMM12 model after ten years: what did we learn about the gut microbiome from a defined microbial community?

This review reflects on ten years of the OMM12 model, a defined community of twelve genome-sequenced, culturable mouse-derived bacterial strains that colonizes reproducibly and stably across hosts. OMM12 reduces the complexity of the native gut microbiota while preserving key ecological and functional traits, and has been used to study colonization resistance and other mechanistic microbiome questions. The authors synthesize what has been learned and likely discuss the model's strengths, limitations, and future directions.

Broad-spectrum in situ genetic reprogramming of native microbiomes.

The authors developed SPARTA, a synthetic phage-based system that packages and delivers large synthetic DNA into diverse native microbial communities in situ, enabling genetic reprogramming of microbiome members without prior isolation. They demonstrate the approach in complex soil, freshwater, and animal-associated microbiomes, showing broad-spectrum delivery and integration. This provides a one-step strategy for editing discrete taxa within intact communities to study or augment microbiome function.

This study integrated metagenomic and metabolomic (GC-MS/LC-MS) analyses of six natural musk samples from forest musk deer to investigate whether musk quality is linked to microbial community composition and metabolic background. A mosaic of bacterial communities and their functional potential across Antarctic moss, lichen and soil.

This study compared bacterial communities living on Antarctic moss, lichen, and soil, finding that the substrate type (moss vs. lichen vs. soil) strongly shapes community composition, while geographic location had little detectable effect. Soil harbored the most diverse communities and the broadest metabolic potential, including nearly complete nitrogen-cycling pathways, whereas the moss-associated community was dominated by Pseudomonadota. These results show that microhabitat is a key driver of microbial community structure and function in Antarctic terrestrial ecosystems.
